title: mTLS service mesh patterns and audit playbook (private deployments)
body:
Purpose:
This note captures recommended mTLS + service-mesh deployment patterns for Redwood Private, the associated firewall/VPC rules, an audit log schema for evidence collection, and a lightweight SIEM-export mapping. It is intended for engineers owning private deployments (VPC/on-prem) and security reviewers.

Scope and goals:
- Provide reproducible, audit-friendly patterns for mutual TLS in two common topologies: gateway-terminating and sidecar-enforced meshes.
- Define firewall/security-group rules and minimal network segmentation patterns that balance production reliability with least-privilege.
- Define an audit log schema and example fields to export to SIEM (Splunk/ELK/Prisma) for evidence automation.
- Provide operational checklists and short runbooks for cert rotation, evidence snapshotting, and incident evidence collection.

Quick summary of recommended topologies (pick one per deployment):
1) Gateway-terminating mTLS (recommended for external-facing workloads):
   - Ingress gateway (edge) terminates external TLS, validates client certs (when applicable), then mTLS from gateway->mesh backends using short-lived workload certs.
   - Benefits: simpler external certificate management, central controls at the edge, easy WAF integration.
   - Risks: gateway is high-value target; ensure hardened bastion and logging.

2) Sidecar-enforced mTLS (recommended for strong east-west security):
   - Every workload runs a sidecar proxy (Envoy/Linkerd) and enforces mTLS peer-to-peer. Control plane issues workload certs (SPIFFE/SPIRE or Istio CA).
   - Benefits: cryptographic identity per workload, easier to implement per-tenant isolation.
   - Risks: higher operational complexity; requires reliable cert issuance and rotation.

3) Hybrid (VPN/Penetration boundary + mesh inside):
   - For very strict regulated deployments, combine a private VPN or Direct Connect into a dedicated VPC perimeter; inside the VPC use a sidecar mTLS mesh.

ASCII diagram (logical):

  [Client] --> LB/Edge-Gateway (TLS terminate) --> Ingress Gateway (mTLS) --> Service A (sidecar) <--> Service B (sidecar)

  Alternate: internal-only deployment
  Admins/VPN --> Private LB --> Sidecar Mesh (mTLS enforced) --> Backing storage/databases (SG-restricted)

Network segmentation and minimal VPC patterns:
- Subnets: public (ingress gateways), app-private (workloads + sidecars), infra (control plane / CA / monitoring), db (data stores, no egress).
- Route tables: no direct routing from app-private to public subnets except via NAT/egress proxies.
- Bastion: management access via private admin subnet + ephemeral jump hosts. Avoid direct internet admin access.

Recommended firewall/security-group rules (examples):
- Ingress gateway SG (AWS security group example):
  - Allow TCP 443 from 0.0.0.0/0 (edge TLS) -- if limited by customer IPs, tighten accordingly.
  - Allow TCP 15021/15090 for mesh health from monitoring SG only.
  - Egress: allow to app-private for mTLS ports (e.g., 15001/15002) only.

- Workload SG (sidecar + app):
  - Ingress: allow TCP 15001 (Envoy inbound) from gateway SG and other workload SGs in app-private (use security group references).
  - Egress: restrict to database SGs on DB ports, to storage endpoints on required ports, and to CA/metadata endpoints for cert fetching.

- DB SG: only accept connections from workload SGs on necessary ports (e.g., 5432).

Cloud firewall / iptables quick examples:
- iptables (host-based guard on bastion or VM):
  iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 22 -s 198.51.100.0/28 -m conntrack --ctstate NEW -j ACCEPT
  iptables -A INPUT -p tcp --dport 15001 -m conntrack --ctstate ESTABLISHED,RELATED -j ACCEPT
  iptables -A INPUT -m conntrack --ctstate INVALID -j DROP

- GCP firewall (v1): allow-ingress rule from load-balancer to gateway instances on 443 only.

mTLS operational model and cert lifecycle:
- Use an automated CA (recommended SPIFFE/SPIRE or Vault PKI) with short-lived certificates (TTL 24h to 7d depending on risk).
- Cert issuance flow: workload requests SVID; CA validates node identity + workload identity; CA issues cert with CN=spiffe://redwood/tenant/<tid>/svc/<svc-name>.
- Rotation: rolling rotation coordinated by control plane: new cert distribution -> sidecar hot-reload -> verification -> revoke old.
- Emergency rekey: CA should support CRL and OCSP or an immediate blocklist push to proxies.

Audit log schema (single-line JSON events recommended for easy SIEM ingestion):
- We recommend emitting a normalized audit/event line for each TLS/mTLS handshake, cert event, and policy decision. Fields:
  - timestamp (iso8601)
  - event_type (handshake | cert_issue | cert_revoke | policy_decision | connection_open | connection_close)
  - tenant_id
  - deployment_id
  - workload (service_name)
  - src_ip
  - src_port
  - dst_ip
  - dst_port
  - src_principal (spiffe id or CN)
  - dst_principal (spiffe id or CN)
  - tls_version
  - tls_cipher
  - cert_fingerprint (sha256)
  - cert_subject
  - cert_issuer
  - cert_valid_from
  - cert_valid_to
  - verdict (allowed | denied | failed_validation)
  - reason (e.g., expired, unknown_issuer, revoked, policy_mismatch)
  - bytes_in
  - bytes_out
  - request_id (application trace id if present)
  - trace_id (distributed trace id if present)

Example event (single-line JSON):
{"timestamp":"2025-01-10T18:24:33Z","event_type":"handshake","tenant_id":"tenant-42","deployment_id":"dp-7","workload":"payments-svc","src_ip":"10.1.5.12","src_port":43210,"dst_ip":"10.1.2.8","dst_port":15001,"src_principal":"spiffe://redwood/tenant/tenant-42/svc/frontend","dst_principal":"spiffe://redwood/tenant/tenant-42/svc/payments","tls_version":"TLS1.3","tls_cipher":"TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256","cert_fingerprint":"ab12...","verdict":"allowed","bytes_in":120,"bytes_out":1024,"request_id":"req-abc123","trace_id":"trace-xyz987"}

SIEM export and mapping guidance:
- Preferred export format: newline-delimited JSON (NDJSON) with the schema above.
- Mapping recommendations: map tenant_id -> customer.id, deployment_id -> host.id, src_principal/dst_principal -> client.user / server.user, request_id -> event.id.
- Splunk: use a dedicated sourcetype (redwood:private:mtls:event). Index into a customer-specific index when required by compliance controls.
- ECS mapping (Elastic Common Schema) suggestion:
  - @timestamp -> timestamp
  - host.id -> deployment_id
  - user.name -> src_principal / dst_principal as appropriate
  - network.transport -> tcp
  - source.ip -> src_ip
  - destination.ip -> dst_ip
  - event.action -> verdict/reason

Log collector example (Logstash-ish config snippet):
  input { file { path => "/var/log/redwood/mtls-events.ndjson" codec => "json" } }
  filter { 
    mutate { rename => { "tenant_id" => "[redwood][tenant_id]" } }
    date { match => [ "timestamp", "ISO8601" ] }
  }
  output { elasticsearch { hosts => ["https://es:9200"] index => "redwood-mtls-%{+YYYY.MM.dd}" } }

Evidence automation and snapshotting
- Goals: produce tamper-evident bundles for compliance review that include: configuration, cert state (chain + current certs), firewall rules, recent audit events (last 72h), and control-plane audit logs.
- Minimal evidence snapshot script steps (example outline):
  1) lock: set a read-only flag on the snapshot job route so no destructive ops are allowed during snapshot (soft).
  2) collect: fetch control-plane cert list (CA metadata endpoint), list of issued SVIDs, current CRLs/OCSP status.
  3) collect: export firewall/security-groups and NACLs (cloud CLI: aws ec2 describe-security-groups etc.).
  4) collect: last 72h NDJSON audit events from local collectors (rotate) and control-plane logs (signed).
  5) sign: create a SHA256 digest of the bundle and sign with an evidence key stored in the enterprise KMS. Record signature metadata.
  6) push: upload to evidence bucket (immutable, versioned) and create an attachment in the incident ticket (Jira/Confluence link).

Example shell pseudo-steps (very condensed):
  # collect cert list
  curl -sS --header "Authorization: Bearer $CAP_TOKEN" https://control-plane.internal/ca/issued | jq . > issued-svids.json
  aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC | jq . > sg.json
  # collect audit events
  tail -n 10000 /var/log/redwood/mtls-events.ndjson > mtls-72h.ndjson
  # bundle and sign
  tar czf evidence-bundle.tgz issued-svids.json sg.json mtls-72h.ndjson
  aws kms sign --key-id alias/evidence-key --message fileb://evidence-bundle.tgz --output text --query Signature > evidence.sig
  aws s3 cp evidence-bundle.tgz s3://redwood-evidence/$DEPLOYMENT/evidence-bundle-$(date +%F).tgz

Operational checklists (short):
- Pre-deployment checklist:
  - CA operational and reachable from control-plane and nodes.
  - Security groups created and validated with least-privilege rules.
  - Logging collectors configured and NDJSON output validated.
  - Evidence bucket configured with object lock & versioning.
  - Smoke test: workload-to-workload mTLS handshake success.

- Weekly health checks:
  - Verify CA cert issuance rates, queue sizes, and failures.
  - Validate no unexpected policy_denied events in audit logs.
  - Check signature freshness on monthly evidence bundles.
  - Verify NTP skew < 2s across cluster (TLS relies on time).

- Incident response quick-run (for suspected MITM/cert compromise):
  1) Rotate CA root key (if required) or immediately revoke affected intermediate.
  2) Push denylists to all proxies and block traffic from suspicious src_principal/ips.
  3) Snapshot current audit events (minute granularity) and collect TLS handshakes surrounding suspect timeframe.
  4) Communicate to customer success/legal per contract.

Operational notes and pitfalls:
- Don’t overexpose certificate metadata in app logs (PII/tenant info). Mask tenant identifiers where necessary for shared logging.
- Beware long-lived certs in CI images or AMIs; bake cert fetching at runtime not in images.
- If using control-plane CA, protect it behind a dedicated management VPC and MFA-required admin flows.

Appendix: short reference commands
- AWS SG export: aws ec2 describe-security-groups --filters Name=vpc-id,Values=$VPC_ID --query 'SecurityGroups[*].{GroupName:GroupName,GroupId:GroupId,IpPermissions:IpPermissions}'
- SPIRE server health: curl -sS http://spire-server:8081/health | jq .
- List issued certs (Vault example): vault list pki/issued | tee issued-certs.txt

Open questions for review:
- SLO for cert issuance latency (target < 200ms for primary CA?).
- Retention policy for NDJSON audit events for regulated customers.
- Should we standardize a tenant_id hashing approach before emitting to shared monitors?

Notes to reviewers:
- This doc is intentionally pragmatic: it mixes runnable snippets and high-level patterns. Replace CA/CLI examples with the customer’s cloud provider conventions when templating.
- For evidence exports to legal/compliance, ensure the evidence bucket and signing key usage is auditable (KMS logs enabled).

-- Marcus
